content: In the past, women were often advised to lower their salt intake during pregnancy as a potential way to reduce the risk of developing pre-eclampsia. However, this practice has largely fallen out of favor. Despite this, it remains important to evaluate the evidence regarding the potential effects of modifying dietary salt intake during pregnancy. The purpose of this review was to examine the impact of altering dietary salt intake during pregnancy on the likelihood of developing pre-eclampsia and its associated complications. To gather relevant data, researchers searched several databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of April 8, 2005), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Issue 1, 2005), and EMBASE (from 2002 to May 2005). The search was later updated on October 1, 2009, and the new findings were added to a section awaiting classification. The review included randomized trials that investigated the effects of either reducing or increasing dietary salt intake during pregnancy. Two authors independently selected the trials for inclusion and extracted the data. The data were analyzed using Review Manager software, and the results were double-checked for accuracy. Ultimately, two trials involving a total of 603 pregnant women were included in the review. Both trials compared the effects of advising women to reduce their dietary salt intake versus advising them to maintain a normal diet. The results showed wide confidence intervals that crossed the line of no effect for all reported outcomes, including the risk of developing pre-eclampsia. Specifically, the relative risk for pre-eclampsia was 1.11, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 0.46 to 2.66. This indicates that there was insufficient evidence to draw reliable conclusions about the effects of reducing dietary salt intake during pregnancy. The authors concluded that, in the absence of clear evidence showing that altering salt intake during pregnancy has any beneficial effect on preventing pre-eclampsia or other outcomes, salt consumption during pregnancy should remain a matter of personal preference. It is worth noting that the citation in the awaiting classification section of the review may influence these conclusions once it is assessed.
